title: ls | wc
subtitle: Two processes, one buffer — the Unix pipeline
why_it_matters: A pipe is how the shell composes programs without a temp file. IR0 allocates an in-memory buffer; the writer blocks when it fills, the reader sees EOF when the last writer closes.

dual_view.kernel:
pipe2()
  ↓ fork ls  (write end)
  ↓ fork wc  (read end)
  ↓ parent wait4

steps.label: The shell sees a pipeline
steps.what_ir0_does: ash parses `ls | wc` and will spawn two children around one pipe.
steps.why_it_matters: Job control and pipelines are why shells fork so often.

steps.label: pipe2
steps.what_ir0_does: sys_pipe2 → pipe_create. Two fds: read end and write end, same buffer, refcounts on each end.
steps.why_it_matters: Fill-a-pipe in Break IR0 is this buffer hitting capacity.

steps.label: Writer: ls
steps.what_ir0_does: Child 1 dups the write end onto stdout, execs ls, lists the directory into the pipe.
steps.why_it_matters: ls never knows about wc — it just writes fd 1.

steps.label: Reader: wc
steps.what_ir0_does: Child 2 dups the read end onto stdin, execs wc, counts until EOF.
steps.why_it_matters: EOF happens when the last writer closes — not when the buffer is empty mid-stream.

steps.label: Parent waits
steps.what_ir0_does: The shell wait4s both children. Prompt returns with wc's numbers.
steps.why_it_matters: Same wait path as fork() — pipelines are fork + pipe + exec, not a special syscall.
